summary: This is a Wikipedia-derived note on boric acid (orthoboric acid, B(OH)3), covering its names, history, and molecular and crystal structure, along with its preparation and reactions such as pyrolysis, aqueous solution behavior, and esterification. It also includes physical properties and toxicology data (LD50 values), and the text is cut off partway through the toxicology section. Boric acid is described as a weak acid used as an antiseptic, insecticide, flame retardant, neutron absorber, and precursor to other boron compounds.
one_line: Overview of boric acid, a weak acid with formula B(OH)3, covering its structure, preparation, reactions, properties and toxicity.
key_facts: Boric acid, more specifically orthoboric acid, is a compound of boron, oxygen and hydrogen with formula B(OH)3.
Boric acid is usually encountered as colorless crystals or a white powder that dissolves in water and occurs in nature as the mineral sassolite.
Boric acid is a weak acid that yields various borate anions and salts and can react with alcohols to form borate esters.
Boric acid is often used as an antiseptic, insecticide, flame retardant, neutron absorber, or precursor to other boron compounds.
Orthoboric acid was first prepared by Wilhelm Homberg (1652-1715) from borax by the action of mineral acids and was given the name sal sedativum Hombergi.
The molar mass of boric acid is 61.83 g/mol, its melting point is 170.9 °C and its boiling point is 300 °C.
Solubility of boric acid in water is 5.7 g/100 mL at 25 °C and 27.53 g/100 mL at 100 °C.
The first proton of boric acid has a pKa of 9.24.
In the triclinic crystal form, layers of B(OH)3 molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds with an O...O separation of 272 pm, and adjacent layers are 318 pm apart.
Boric acid can be prepared by reacting borax (sodium tetraborate decahydrate) with a mineral acid such as hydrochloric acid.
When heated above 140 °C, orthoboric acid yields metaboric acid (HBO2) with loss of one water molecule, and further heating to about 530 °C leads to boron trioxide.
The oral LD50 of boric acid in rats is 2660 mg/kg, and the Merck Index states the rat oral LD50 is 5.14 g/kg.
The Merck Index indicates that 5 to 20 g/kg of boric acid has produced death in adult humans.
